#646. Over a decade of atmospheric data from NASA's Curiosity rover hints at small amounts of surface water on Mars

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (93 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Phys

Over a decade of atmospheric data from NASA's Curiosity rover hints at small amounts of surface water on Mars

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (93 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Phys

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that NASA's Curiosity rover has been collecting data about Mars' thin, carbon dioxide–rich atmosphere since 2012. Now, a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences has analyzed over a decade of this data to determine whether the daily and seasonal changes in Mars' atmosphere could be explained by known processes, including the freezing and release of carbon dioxide at its poles. What they found suggests a process involving water either attached to soil grains or in extremely thin, liquid-like films at the surface.

Industry observers note that gold nanoclusters, composed of a small number of gold atoms, can exhibit optical, electronic and catalytic properties distinct from those of bulk gold. One intriguing family consists of carbon-centered gold(I) clusters, in which a carbon atom is surrounded by several gold atoms. Unlike the familiar four-coordinate carbon in methane, the central carbon in these clusters can be coordinated by five or even six gold atoms.

According to recent reports, over the past 800,000 years, Earth's history has been marked by dramatic shifts in climate, swinging from warm periods to cold, when large ice sheets covered much of the Northern Hemisphere and sea ice greatly expanded. The transition between the two climates is paced by the Earth's orbit with respect to the sun, but changes in the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2), a greenhouse gas, also affect global temperatures. By understanding how CO2 is exchanged between the atmosphere and the ocean, scientists hope to apply that knowledge to future climate scenarios.

#626. Industry News: 10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker

Industry News: 10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that crime dramas often attract substantial stars, and MobLand is no exception.
  • While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family.
  • Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that crime dramas often attract substantial stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other demonstrates mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

It has been revealed that another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's manufacturer town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

According to recent reports, A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated proposal to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates latest maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Tech giant all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other highlights on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

Industry observers note that the great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone.
  • According to recent reports, according to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple indicates that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages.
  • Sources indicate that it's not clear what's causing the complications with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time.

According to recent reports, if you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone. As of early Tuesday afternoon, Downdetector shows user reports of concerns across multiple Apple services. While Apple's System Status page initially indicated far fewer issues than Downdetector users reported, the site has since updated to reflect general outages.

According to recent reports, according to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple indicates that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages. Apple says that the App Store and Apple Music "may be slow or unavailable," while AppleCare purchase is presently unavailable. The company's System Status page reveals an "glitch" with iCloud Account & Sign In. Other services with user reports on Downdetector, including the Apple Card, Apple Online Store, and Apple Business, read as "Available." Apple also says there was an outage with the Volume Purchase Program, but that has since been resolved.

Sources indicate that it's not clear what's causing the complications with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time. However, the timing is odd. It comes after a number of banks experienced outages on Monday, as well as Microsoft's massive outage the previous week. In addition to all of these outages, the FAA unexpectedly grounded all U.S. flights on Friday, for only the third time in the agency's history.

As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft.

Sources indicate that the event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth. And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).

NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.

Industry observers note that to celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code: NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence.

Sources indicate that the spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said.

NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making.

The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1. At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes.

Industry observers note that launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2, is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.).

Sources indicate that the public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission. On Thursday (Nov. 19) at 12 p.m. EST (1700 GMT), NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with Voyager mission team members and NASA leadership.

Recent findings suggest that the discussion will cover the current status of both Voyager spacecraft, the unique scientific observations they continue to collect in interstellar space and the engineering challenges involved in keeping the nearly 50-year-old probes operational. A question-and-answer session with members of the media and audience will follow. NASA will also offer a preview of an upcoming Voyager documentary planned for release in 2027, coinciding with the mission's 50th anniversary.

In a recent development, for a mission that has carried humanity's message into interstellar space for nearly half a century, the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day” offers a chance for people back on Earth to mark just how far these pioneering spacecraft have traveled. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, new photographers looking for inspiration often start with an app like VSCO. The popular mobile app, debuted more than a decade ago, is known for one-click presets that emulate film and make it easy to elevate a photograph before posting it to social media. But as newbie shutterbugs level up their craft, they often graduate to an app like Adobe Lightroom and its more professional tool set.

VSCO's pitch is simple: Keep photographers in the ecosystem by building a desktop app to rival Lightroom. On Tuesday, the company declared that its Studio Pro Desktop app is officially landing on macOS, following the launch of Studio Pro on iOS earlier this year. Neither version is available on Android or Windows, though the San Francisco–based company plans to port the apps in the future.

“We're helping shape these folks in their formative years,” VSCO CEO Eric Wittman tells WIRED. “We've got to keep giving them more bricks to build upon their own personal, creative journey—not just their creative journey, but also help them build a career.”.

In a recent development, the desktop client is one part of VSCO's growing portfolio that caters to full-time photographers. Subscribing to VSCO One, for example, nets you access to Studio Pro, additional presets, and VSCO Workspace—a customer relationship management tool for handling contracts, booking, and scheduling. It also includes VSCO Galleries to send finished work directly to clients and VSCO Sites, a portfolio website builder to find upcoming clients. All of these apps and services rolled out in the past year.

Access to the broad suite costs $500 a year, or you can get the Studio Pro mobile and desktop apps alone with a VSCO Pro membership for $5 per month ($60 annually). There is also a free tier, but some tools are locked behind the subscription. (Naturally, the original VSCO app is still around for enthusiasts.).

In a recent development, the Studio Pro Desktop app is speedy, features more than 200 presets, and supports RAW editing for 20 camera brands. Batch editing is the highlight, letting photographers edit up to 500 images simultaneously to speed up workflows while preserving the original files. Previews are rendered in real time, and at the end, users can export the final images directly to VSCO Galleries (or wherever they'd like).

I've been trying the app for a few weeks, and it is snappy. It loads RAW files quickly, and it even supports keyboard shortcuts. The sheer breadth of presets is also really nice, even if I tend to tweak colors myself. But there's a catch. If you're like me and coming from Lightroom, you'll miss a few features that Studio Pro Desktop doesn't offer yet. For example, Masking, Curves, and the Erase function (aka the spot removal tool) are “coming soon.”.

In a recent development, “We want to be simple, intentionally, but we want to be powerful with our tools,” indicates Kyle Hale, VSCO's senior product manager. He says the app will feature around 70 percent of what people need for desktop editing, with the rest coming through regular software updates. While he doesn't expect full parity with a competitor like Lightroom by the first quarter of 2027, Studio Pro Desktop will have “the meat of what those programs offer.”.

Sources indicate that companies like Adobe have heavily leaned into generative AI in their creative editing tools. While VSCO uses AI and machine-learning models in some tools like the upcoming Erase and retouch tools, the firm notes it doesn't train its own models on anything that people post on the VSCO app. VSCO also relies on some third-party models, like those from Black Forest Labs, but it has agreements in place that third parties cannot train on its user data.

“I don't think all AI is bad,” Wittman says. “But to be very, very clear: Generative AI, or if you're replacing the photographer—like what you're seeing with what Meta is doing, what Adobe's doing, like almost every other tech giant is doing—we are not doing that. We stand by and champion photographers first and foremost, and that's not going to change.”.

On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.

In a recent development, surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the major liftoff.

It has been revealed that first Surveyor 6 introduced from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.

In a recent development, surveyor 6 revealed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.

In a recent development, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft rolled out to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.

Sources indicate that the probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.

Industry observers note that but a lunar liftoff? That was something latest.

"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.

The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.

But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.

In a recent development, "This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation.".

Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.

Curiosity’s past several weeks have been very focused on drilling and analysis of the “Basque Lakes” and “Nazca” samples. As we climb higher on Mount Sharp, we’ll continue to use many of our less resource intensive science instruments like APXS, ChemCam, MAHLI, and Mastcam to document the chemistry and textures of the rocks we encounter while making purposeful upward progress. These measurements allow us to document changes in the environments that formed the rocks and that altered them over time.

The two areas we explored this week had rocks that were crisscrossed by lots of small, regular sized polygons surrounded by raised ridges. This texture was very similar to the rocks we encountered a few months ago slightly lower on the mountain. Those unique textures really surprised us when we first saw them, and we’ve been spending time as a science team discussing how they may have formed. Polygonal textures like these can form under a variety of different conditions including shrinkage of the surface when water is lost from minerals, temperature cycling, or compaction and expansion after being buried and exposed. The data Curiosity collected this week give us more clues about the genesis of these features and what they reveal about the evolution of Mars’ habitability. We’ll also get information about the composition of the cements that form the raised ridges around the polygons.

In the orbital view of our future route, I can see the layers that we’ll reach next week or the week after have textures very similar to where we first saw the amazing field of polygons. So I’m guessing we’ll continue to encounter polygons in the next couple drives, and that they’ll look more dramatic and expansive with each drive. But this is just a guess! After over 5,000 sols of exploring with Curiosity I’ve learned Mars is full of surprises, so I’m really looking forward to seeing what’s up ahead in the upcoming future and testing if my guess is correct.

Recent findings suggest that the failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance remarked today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA noted in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's upgrade.

In a recent development, the two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which introduced in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

According to recent reports, on both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security debuts with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.).

Recent findings suggest that that work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA stated in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the tech giant wrote in today's update.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's upgrade did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's Newly introduced Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is at the moment recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.).

It has been revealed that NASA prepares to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Industry observers note that vulcan's grounding is a substantial deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and Fresh Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX looks to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's blueprint to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 releases on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

Industry observers note that the other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 releases (not including Sunday's failure).

After days of political fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, President Donald Trump is defending commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.

Last week, Lutnick came under fire from treasury secretary Scott Bessent for not aggressively imposing export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

But Trump’s defense of Lutnick, sources tell WIRED, reflects the president's own view that allowing the sale of some advanced AI chips to China can keep China reliant on US technology and simultaneously boost US tech stocks.

Lutnick “was doing that because if you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump mentioned ahead of a multiday trip to Asia and a meeting on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Trump convened an Oval Office meeting on November 5 to discuss the political fallout from Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive whom some in the US government believe was recruited to spy for China, according to two sources briefed on the discussion.

Megaspeed received advanced AI chips manufactured by Nvidia through several layers of companies that started with a subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese server conglomerate called Inspur, The Latest York Times has reported.

In the meeting, the sources say, Bessent confronted Lutnick, asking why Megaspeed was not added to the entity list faster, given that secretary of state Marco Rubio and US trade representative Jamieson Greer, among others, had already agreed it was the correct move.

Lutnick responded that he would defer to Trump and would add Megaspeed to the entity list if that was what the president wanted, the sources say.

But Trump settled on a third approach: for Lutnick to work on introducing a upcoming interim trade rule to stop Chinese AI labs from using advanced AI chips remotely by leasing their compute power from data centers in Southeast Asia.

In a statement to WIRED, a White House spokesperson noted the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.” (Superintelligence, or SI, is the administration’s term for artificial intelligence.).

It has been revealed that A senior White House official added that Trump has been adamant that Chinese firms cannot acquire the most advanced Nvidia chips, known as Blackwells and Rubins. Those are different from the H200-type chips, built on previous-generation Hopper architecture, that Megaspeed was acquiring.

According to recent reports, lutnick’s position appears to have been based on a series of considerations, the sources say. For one, Megaspeed has already had the chips for months, and blacklisting the company would be akin to playing whack-a-mole unless the administration dealt with the underlying issue of Chinese firms getting remote access to US chips.

Meanwhile, Lutnick has moved cautiously on any latest export restrictions—essentially waiting to get explicit approval from Trump—after he faced heavy criticism in 2025 for expanding restrictions against firms with Chinese ties, the sources said.

In September 2025, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security started aggressively using the so-called affiliates rule, which automatically extends trade restrictions to any company that is 50 percent owned by a company already on the US entity list or the military end-user list.

But the move prompted immediate retaliation by China, which suspended exports of critical rare earth metals to the US and, the sources said, prompted a wave of internal criticism accusing the Commerce Department of having sparked a trade war.

After the Busan summit at the end of October 2025, where Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping agreed to a trade truce, the White House instructed Commerce to halt the use of the affiliates rule and clear new export controls in advance, the sources said.

The suspension of the affiliates rule—which came almost as soon as it was implemented—may have had a knock-on effect on companies like Megaspeed, one person familiar with deliberations said.

Inspur, the Chinese server conglomerate connected to Megaspeed, operated a subsidiary called Aivres, which, as a California-based company, could legally buy restricted Nvidia chips without triggering direct export bans and ship them internationally to Southeast Asia.

In total, Aivres transferred billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips, including the powerful H200 chips, to Megaspeed’s subsidiaries.

Instead of shipping the physical chips into China, Megaspeed hosted servers at data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia—then rented out compute power to major Chinese companies. A spokesperson for Aivres noted in a statement that the tech giant complies with all US export controls.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • In a recent development, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • Recent findings suggest that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

In a recent development, as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

Recent findings suggest that you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This substantial-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and organization also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

In a recent development, horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

It has been revealed that I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley indicates up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

Recent findings suggest that there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

According to recent reports, I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

Sources indicate that it doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

It has been revealed that the animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

In a recent development, the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

  • It has been revealed that in response, Waymo states it has stopped highway driving in all of its markets.
  • Industry observers note that the ban follows two recent concerning incidents, California DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman wrote in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waymo self-driving taxis are no longer driving on highways after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned its vehicles from state freeway operations. The ban, which the DMV claims began on November 11, comes after the department determined that Waymo’s freeway driving poses “an imminent hazard to public safety.”.

It has been revealed that in response, Waymo states it has stopped highway driving in all of its markets. The company may continue testing its vehicles on non-California highways with safety operators behind the wheel.

Industry observers note that the ban follows two recent concerning incidents, California DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman wrote in a statement. In one, three Waymos entered an active highway construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula. The other was captured in a viral video showing a Waymo vehicle interfering with California Highway Patrol cars on a San Francisco highway as they tried to enforce a “traffic break” as workers cleared debris from a crash.

Industry observers note that groveman said the California ban will remain in place until Waymo has proved that it has “taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies” that led to the incidents. It’s unclear how long that process will take.

In a written statement to WIRED, Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher mentioned the firm is “working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.” Waymo vehicles will continue to operate on surface streets in the 15 metros where it offers taxi service, including portions of Los Angeles, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

Recent findings suggest that this is the second time Waymo has publicly restricted its freeway operations after beginning to transport passengers on them last year. In June, the company recalled its software after federal regulators found that its system failed to recognize highway construction zones. Regulators with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration cited several incidents in April and May in which Waymo cars drove past ramp closure signs and into active lane closures. The events did not lead to collisions or injuries.

The NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Recent findings suggest that last week, the agency noted it was examining whether another Waymo recall software fix had actually solved its robotaxis’ safety complications. This recall, which occurred last December, was tied to incidents in which Waymo cars repeatedly drove by stopped school buses with their lights on and/or stop arms extended.

Recent findings suggest that self-driving cars have struggled with construction zones for at least a decade. The zones can look and be arranged differently based on what sort of construction is being done and where. While humans can easily understand bollards, placards, and blinking arrows, the lack of hard-and-fast rules has proven difficult to reliably program into driving software. The matter is especially hazardous at freeway speeds, where workers exist alongside fast-moving car traffic.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first shoes with Nike’s newly introduced Tuned Air technology will be available for runners starting in late 2027.﻿.

The first shoes with Nike’s newly introduced Tuned Air technology will be available for runners starting in late 2027.﻿.

In a recent development, in 2024, Nike declared its Air Max 1000 that were manufactured using a 3D-printing process resulting in a shoe that had a uniform silhouette but varying areas of support and flexibility throughout. The tech giant is now doing something similar with its iconic air-filled soles using its fresh Tuned Air technology. While previously the level of cushioning in Nike Air shoes was uniform across the entire sole, a new manufacturing process can produce multiple air pockets with varying levels of cushioning and stability.

Nike has been putting air pockets into its shoes for nearly 50 years as a way to increase comfort and cushioning while making them lighter. Its air pockets have even found their way into apparel as a way to improve insulation by trapping body heat, but Nike aims to use its new Tuned Air technology as a way to customize the cushioning experience in its shoes and tailor them to specific athletes and sports. The first shoes featuring the technology are expected to arrive in late 2027 and will be targeted at runners.

Industry observers note that while one of Nike’s earliest successes was track shoes with a grip design inspired by a waffle iron, the company credits the “vibrant colors on magazine covers” as the inspiration for its latest shoe technology. A Tuned Air sole is manufactured using a “proprietary digital print and selective lamination process” where an ink is applied in specific patterns that define where the layers bond to each other. This process can be used to create internal pockets in an unlimited combination of shapes and sizes, and by fine-tuning how much air is in each of those pockets, some parts of the sole can feel firmer while others feel softer.

The Tuned Air technology will not only allow Nike to highly customize the fit and feel of air sole shoes for different sports, it will also help keep the benefits of the custom tuning consistent across different sizes. The fresh manufacturing process will also help reduce the amount of time it takes Nike to go from a concept for a new shoe to a final design ready for production. “Prototypes that once took three weeks can now be made in three days,” the company claims in a release today. That gives Nike’s designers more time to refine new shoes, and more opportunity to experiment.

#604. Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova

Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
  • Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did.
  • Sources indicate that however, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.

Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole.

Sources indicate that however, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes.

The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), remarked in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova.

"These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

According to recent reports, right now, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs.

Sources indicate that chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over the past 10 years.

This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

According to recent reports, the researchers also looked at the spin rates of black holes in mergers, a telltale signature of how they formed. This revealed that 10-solar-mass black holes seemed to have a distinct range of spin speeds. This indicates a common origin, perhaps the implosion of a massive star without a supernova explosion.

According to recent reports, "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred concluded. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Physical Review D.

NICER Status Updates

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) telescope on the International Space Station has ended science operations.
  • The mission and space station teams are now focused on prepares to finalize NICER’s 8-year archive of X-ray science observations and decommission and detach the telescope from its perch near the station’s starboard solar array.
  • Sources indicate that in June 2025, NICER was suddenly unable to swivel side-to-side beyond its current orientation, which limited its ability to track cosmic objects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s NICER Telescope Ends Science Operations.

After studying the universe for six and a half years beyond its initial mission, NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) telescope on the International Space Station has ended science operations.

The mission and space station teams are now focused on prepares to finalize NICER’s 8-year archive of X-ray science observations and decommission and detach the telescope from its perch near the station’s starboard solar array.

Sources indicate that in June 2025, NICER was suddenly unable to swivel side-to-side beyond its current orientation, which limited its ability to track cosmic objects. The team paused data collection to investigate the problem.

Sources indicate that robotic cameras on the outside of the station collected photographs of NICER that helped eliminate external causes. After an extensive investigation, engineers think an internal motor has failed, limiting the telescope’s motion.

Launched in 2017, NICER embarked on an initial 18-month prime mission. Since then, it has made groundbreaking measurements of neutron stars, which contain the densest matter in the universe that we can measure, and revolutionized our understanding of black holes, active galaxies, and other mysterious phenomena in our universe.

The telescope also successfully demonstrated the potential of pulsar-based spacecraft navigation in X-rays that could be used for travel to Mars and beyond. Closer to home, technology developed to test NICER before launch is being incorporated into prototype portable CT scanners, materials analysis systems, and other applications.

Science Observations Remain Paused for NASA’s NICER Telescope.

It has been revealed that science operations by NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer), an X-ray telescope on the International Space Station, remain paused as the team continues to evaluate the telescope’s systems after an glitch developed with one of its motors. The motor is unable to move NICER beyond its current position side to side, and the telescope’s status has not changed since operations were halted June 17.

The primary goal is to move NICER into its stowed configuration in case it needs to accommodate space station activities, though the current placement does not pose a safety issue to the station or crew. The team currently does not have a timeframe for returning to science operations.

Industry observers note that photos taken by robotic cameras outside the station are helping eliminate external causes for the problem. Now the team is coordinating with space station personnel to perform troubleshooting maneuvers and determine potential causes within the payload.

Since it began observing the X-ray universe in 2017, NICER has successfully demonstrated a form of deep space navigation that could be used for travel to Mars and beyond.

It has been revealed that designed for a prime mission of 18 months and now in its eighth year of operations, NICER has made groundbreaking measurements of neutron stars, which contain the densest matter in the universe that we can measure, and revolutionized our understanding of black holes, active galaxies, and other mysterious phenomena in our universe. Technology developed to test NICER before launch is being incorporated into prototype portable CT scanners, communications systems, and several other applications on Earth for the benefit of all.

NASA’s NICER Telescope Suspends Science Operations.

NASA’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer), an X-ray telescope on the International Space Station, has paused observations due to a problem with one of the motors that drives its ability to track cosmic objects.

Industry observers note that the NICER team paused operations June 17 when performance degradation in the motor began affecting science observations. Engineers are investigating the cause and potential solutions.

The telescope was installed near the space station’s starboard solar array in 2017. The NICER mission has successfully demonstrated a form of deep space navigation that could be used for travel to Mars and beyond. It has also made groundbreaking measurements of neutron stars, which contain the densest matter in the universe that we can measure, and revolutionized our understanding of black holes, active galaxies, and other mysterious phenomena in our universe.

Following Repair, NASA’s NICER Improves Daytime Measurements.

A NASA X-ray telescope on the International Space Station called NICER, or Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer, has regained additional daytime observation capabilities thanks to repairs completed during a spacewalk and a reconfiguration of its detectors.

Sources indicate that in May 2023, NICER developed a light leak in which unwanted sunlight began entering the instrument. Photos taken from inside the space station revealed several small areas of damage to the telescope’s thin thermal shields, which block sunlight while allowing X-rays through to the detectors. Nighttime observations were unaffected, and with operational adjustments, the NICER team was able to recover about 20% of station daytime observations.

In a recent development, in January, NASA astronaut Nick Hague installed nine patches to cover the largest areas of damage during a spacewalk. After resuming science operations, the NICER team determined the overall level of sunlight inside NICER had substantially reduced. Still, it experienced more visible-light interference than expected.

Close-up, high-resolution photos from the spacewalk allowed the team to see additional small holes and cracks in the thermal shields that were not previously visible. These accounted for the remaining sunlight intrusion.

After further analysis, the NICER team developed a novel approach to regaining additional daytime data collection.

In a recent development, each X-ray that hits a NICER detector generates electrical charge that is sensed by a measurement/power unit (MPU). After so many hits, the detector resets — like emptying a cup before it overflows.

Sunlight can also create charge that accumulates in the detector, adding water to the metaphorical cup. There was so much sunlight entering NICER that the detectors were filling up with charge and resetting thousands of times for every X-ray detection. It overwhelmed the MPU’s ability to process the valid X-ray events.

Hague’s repair in January reduced the amount of sunlight entering NICER, which enabled the team to reconfigure the MPUs to ignore the sunlight-generated resets. After initial testing on the ground, the team updated one MPU before switching all seven. The changeover was completed March 12.

In combination with the patches, the reconfiguration has allowed NICER to return to collecting observations during more than 70% of station daytime, as the telescope continues to help us better understand the X-ray universe, including neutron stars, black holes, and other energetic phenomena. The team continues to look for more opportunities to improve NICER’s operations.

NASA’s NICER Continues Science Operations Post Repair.

Sources indicate that NASA crew aboard the International Space Station installed patches to the agency’s NICER (Neutron star Interior Composition Explorer) mission during a spacewalk on Jan. 16. NICER, an X-ray telescope perched near the station’s starboard solar array, resumed science operations later the same day.

The patches cover areas of NICER’s thermal shields where damage was discovered in May 2023. These thin filters block sunlight while allowing X-rays to pass through. After the discovery, the NICER team restricted their observations during the station’s daytime to avoid overwhelming the mission’s sensitive detectors. Nighttime observations were unaffected, and the team was able to continue collecting data for the science community to make groundbreaking measurements using the instrument’s full capabilities.

Industry observers note that the repair went according to plan. Data since collected indicates the detectors behind the patched areas are performing better than before during station night, and the overall level of sunlight inside NICER during the daytime is reduced substantially.

It has been revealed that while NICER experiences less interference from sunlight than before, after analyzing initial data, the team has determined the telescope still experiences more interference than expected. The installed patches cover areas of known damage identified using astronomical observations and from photos taken by both external robotic cameras and astronauts inside the space station. Measurements collected since the repair and close-up, high-resolution photos obtained during the spacewalk are providing upcoming information that may point the way toward further daytime data collection.

In the meantime, NICER continues operations with its full measurement capabilities during orbit night to enable further trailblazing discoveries in time domain and multimessenger astrophysics.

Sunlight ‘Leak’ Impacting NASA’s NICER Telescope, Science Continues.

It has been revealed that on Tuesday, May 22, NASA’s NICER (Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer), an X-ray telescope on the International Space Station, developed a “light leak,” in which unwanted sunlight enters the instrument. While analyzing incoming data since then, the team identified an impact to daytime observations. Nighttime observations seem to be unaffected.

The team suspects that at least one of the thin thermal shields on NICER’s 56 X-ray Concentrators has been damaged, allowing sunlight to reach its sensitive detectors.

It has been revealed that to mitigate the effects on measurements, the NICER team has limited daytime observations to objects far away from the Sun’s position in the sky. The team has also updated commands to NICER that automatically lower its sensitivity during the orbital day to reduce the effects from sunlight contamination. The team is evaluating these changes and assessing additional measures to reduce the impact on science observations.

To date, more than 300 scientific papers have used NICER observations, and the team is confident that NICER will continue to produce world-class science.
