According to recent reports, before there was the iPhone Duo, there was the Z Fold 8. Not by much — just a few months — but Samsung beat Apple to market with a passport-shaped foldable. It’s a little thinner, lighter, and narrower than the Duo, and that makes a real difference in how comfortable it is to use for long stretches of time. It’s not rated for the same level of dust resistance as the Duo, and it doesn’t feel quite as “premium,” but apps make better use of the cover screen. The more I hold it, the more I think Apple needs to take a page out of Samsung’s book here. — Allison Johnson, senior reviewer.

Recent findings suggest that 3D printing is finally something I can recommend to just about anyone with space for a 30-inch cube in their garage, because the Bambu Lab P2S Combo is the easiest printing experience I’ve touched. It prints beautifully out of the box but, more importantly, it keeps on printing with minimal care, maintenance, or fuss. I can leave rolls of colorful filament inside for months, then press a button on my phone to print, because the bundled AMS keeps them dry and automatically loads each one. Technically the P2S arrived in 2025, but I’d never buy a just-released 3D printer: I spent a year and over 1,700 hours of print time (and counting) to be sure of my recommendation. Wish Bambu treated the open-source community better, though. — Sean Hollister, senior editor.

Sources indicate that when The Verge decided to do a Best of 2026, my mind immediately jumped to the nerdiest thing I’ve tested all year — a dongle that lets you power aging gadgets with the same USB-C cables that charge your laptop and phone. Lose your SNES power brick? Want to make a desktop monitor portable? Want to make a Game Boy run forever? Werewolf VFLEX can make those happen, and so much more. It’s like having a universal AC adapter, one you don’t even need to plug into the wall, because USB-C batteries are amazing. — Sean Hollister, senior editor.

It’s no surprise that, given its provenance, the Fitbit Air is an excellent fitness tracker, even if its tracking capabilities don’t go as in depth as other devices. For $100, the Air comes with a thinner and more comfortable strap than Whoop’s bands, with a design that lets the sensor module be easily removed and swapped into other straps. Battery life is excellent, requiring just a handful of charges each month while the Air tracks metrics like steps, heart rate, sleep, blood oxygen, and cardio load. All of that data is available through the Google Health app without a subscription, but for $100 you can upgrade to Google Health Premium, which adds access to video workouts, adaptive fitness plans, and an AI health coach that can share summaries of your day or night and answer questions about your health. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter.

According to recent reports, I usually regret my TikTok shop purchases. Not this one. I was tired of filling my journals with muddy, blue-tinged photos from HP Sprocket that faded over time. The Liene Pearl N200 Pro uses dye sublimation, so the colors are super vivid. The app is easy to use, and it comes with 50 sheets and five ink cartridges. You can usually find it for $100 to $120, and refills cost just $25 for 50 sheets. That’s pretty affordable — especially if you love scrapbooking. — Victoria Song, senior reviewer.

According to recent reports, the Oura Ring 5 is thinner and lighter than the Oura Ring 4. The metal finish is more durable than Oura’s previous models, so nicks and scratches should be less of an issue. The case also adds support for on-the-go wireless charging, but unfortunately it’s sold separately. This year’s Oura Ring also dropped the smallest and largest size options. The Oura Ring 5 is still the best smart ring on the market, especially if you’re upgrading from an older model or are new to smart rings. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer.

According to recent reports, 2026 is the year nearly every TV manufacturer released an RGB LED TV, which uses individual red, green, and blue LEDs to provide the backlight instead of a field of blue or white LEDs. The Sony Bravia 9 II is the best of the bunch, with accurate, vibrant color; the incredible processing that Sony is known for; and a really cool lenticular screen on the stand that hides the cables behind it. The first generation of a latest technology is always a bit tricky, but Sony revealed that an RGB LED TV can be done right. — John Higgins, TV & audio senior reviewer.

Industry observers note that when Sony debuted its WH-1000XM4C wireless headphones in October, there was a certain amount of smug satisfaction enjoyed by those of us who still prefer Sony’s six-year-old WH-1000XM4 headphones over its successors. Sony made significant design changes with the WH-1000XM5 and then walked a few of them back with the WH-1000XM6. Both have better active noise cancellation and battery life than Sony’s latest, but the new XM4C resurrects the XM4’s comfortable, compact folding design with a replaceable battery, so loyal fans of the original can enjoy the new version for years to come. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter.

The Liberty 5 Pro set a new bar for call quality this year. The Verge’s John Higgins said they delivered the best in-call noise canceling he’s ever heard, even compared with pricier headphones like Apple’s AirPods Pro 3. They run on Anker’s new Thus chip and feature 9.2mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and IP55 water resistance. The case also has a built-in display to rapidly change settings like ANC or check the Liberty 5 Pro’s battery life, with separate icons for each earbud and the case itself. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer.

There’s plenty about the Studio Display XDR to find interesting: It’s the first Apple 5K monitor with a mini-LED panel and quantum dots that has a peak brightness of 2,000 nits, it has an adaptive refresh rate up to 120Hz, and it has a bunch of color-accurate reference modes for a wide range of professional uses. But what got me most excited was the inclusion of Apple’s CMF 2026 color-matching function for its two general picture-mode presets. It’s a upcoming display standard developed as an alternative to CIE 1931, the standard for the past 80 years, which can cause colors to look different across multiple narrow-band display technologies like OLED and mini-LED with quantum dots. Apple CMF 2026 aims to fix that, and I’m here for it. — John Higgins, TV & audio senior reviewer.

The MacBook Neo, despite running on an iPhone chip, works pretty darn well as a MacBook, and that’s mostly all I need to say. Yes, it now starts at $699 instead of $599 because of RAMageddon, so it’s not as good of a deal as it was when it rolled out. But it’s a very functional laptop, still has a great keyboard and (mechanical!) trackpad, and comes in fun colors. Apple hit it out of the park with the Neo. — Jay Peters, senior reporter.

Sources indicate that framework’s Laptop 13 Pro is my ideal all-purpose Windows laptop (or Linux, if you’re inclined). It’s portable, powerful, dabbles in 1080p gaming, and it’s even user-upgradable and repairable. It’s the Framework formula many of us have come to love, like those precious modular ports, but with a major step up in quality-of-life features: a haptic trackpad, a nice touchscreen, and a much-improved build. Its biggest fault is its price. That’s the toll RAMageddon has taken on everything this year — it just hit a smaller manufacturer like Framework harder. Yes, Framework chose an extra-pricey component in LPCAMM2 memory, but that’s also part of why the 13 Pro is so cool and forward-looking. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer.

Recent findings suggest that I was so head over heels for the Ricoh GR IV Monochrome when I reviewed it that I recently bought one. A black-and-white-only fixed-lens camera is super niche, but for this photo nerd, it’s the perfect “artsy” pocket camera. I take it with me everywhere, even with my larger cameras during Verge events or wedding shoots. It’s a palate cleanser for everything from slice-of-life family snapshots to Newly introduced York City street photography. I could achieve that with black-and-white film, but I inevitably fall off using my analog cameras. They say the best camera is the one you have with you, and the GR IV Monochrome is now always with me and always a delight. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer.

The Nape Pro is the most unusual and best gadget I bought this year. It’s a bar-shaped device with six customizable buttons and a small trackball in the middle. I put it horizontally below my space bar, and once I tweaked the button layout, it became a daily driver. It feels like a cross between a trackpad and what I wish the TrackPoint on my ThinkPad was. The Nape Pro works over Bluetooth, USB-C, or 2.4GHz and supports up to 1000Hz polling. Battery life is fantastic, and it’s fully customizable. I still use a mouse at the big desk, but the Nape Pro is now as key to my portable setup as my laptop stand and keyboard. — Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor.

Xteink redefined how small an e-reader can be, and while the tech giant released several models in 2026 — including the X3, X4, and X4 Classic — the X4 Pro is the best of the bunch. It’s the company’s only model to include lighting and a touchscreen, which makes navigating Xteink’s software, or an excellent third-party alternative, much easier than using buttons alone. At $99, the X4 Pro is Xteink’s most expensive e-reader, and it doesn’t include access to an online bookstore, but with a 4.26-inch screen, you can slip it in a pocket alongside your phone. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter.

Months after reviewing it, I’m still a huge fan of Valve’s second-generation Steam Controller. It’s comfortable to hold for hours-long gaming sessions, has enough battery life that I never really think about it, and I love how I can customize nearly everything about the controller on a per-game basis inside Steam. If I have one knock against the controller, it’s that I don’t use the big touchpads all that often to replicate a mouse — but I have used them as giant buttons, which can be surprisingly useful in a pinch. I think I’ll be gaming with it for years to come.— Jay Peters, senior reporter.

The Peak Design City Bags offer a unique way to hang them up wherever you are. They have a hook so you can hang them off a table and keep them off the dirty ground. The Verge’s Thomas Ricker, who reviewed the bags, noted they made him a convert: “It beats setting a bag on the dirty ground or hanging it off the back of the chair where it will inevitably slide onto the floor, and it’s far better than holding a bag on your sweaty lap on a hot summer day.” He said they fit squarely in the everyday carry sweet spot for most people. — Jay Peters, senior reporter.

According to recent reports, I love ridiculous laptops, and there’s nothing quite as over-the-top as dual-screen models like Asus’ Zephyrus Duo and Zenbook Duo. The wildly expensive Zephyrus Duo gaming laptop is the perfect embodiment of this extravagant formula, with a mobile RTX 5090 GPU, dual 16-inch OLEDs, and a $5,500 price tag. It’s a marvel of maximalism. The more practical version is the latest Zenbook Duo — with its pair of 14-inch OLEDs and Intel Panther Lake chip — which is still pricey at $2,700, but no slouch for 1080p gaming on its integrated GPU. I wish these kinds of laptops had more accessible price points because they are an absolute treat to use. The more screens, the merrier. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer.

Recent findings suggest that the Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 power bank is the latest update in its line of ultralight battery packs. Nitecore has made a name for itself among endurance athletes and backpackers who want to pack as light as possible while still having enough power to recharge a phone and a smartwatch. The NB10000 has IPX7 protection to withstand rain or light immersion, two USB-C ports, a 10,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, and enough juice to top up an iPhone 15 Pro twice. It costs $84, which is a lot more than what you’d spend on a standard 10,000mAh battery, but it’s worth it for anyone who wants a thin and light battery that lasts. Oh, and did we mention there are RGB lights around the USB-C ports? — Todd Haselton, deputy reviews editor.

Few products are truly perfect all-rounders in the smart home world, but Aqara’s G400 video doorbell comes close. It works with every platform, has local storage, and offers on-device AI to alert you to people at your door. It can record 24/7 because it’s hardwired, which also makes it a good choice for reliability, and there’s even the option of power over ethernet. It looks like a giant Mars bar on my front door, but I can forgive it for this because it does everything else very well. And at only $100, it is one of those rarities in tech today: a good product that’s affordable. — Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior reviewer.

Recent findings suggest that the Schlage Sense Pro is the smartest lock on the block, thanks to ultra-wideband hands-free unlocking. With your phone in your pocket or bag, it can unlock as you approach, so you can just open the door — no need for keys or fiddling with an app. It’s like stepping into the future. While there are a couple of other UWB locks out there, the Schlage is my favorite because of its sleek, all-metal design, lack of a keyhole, and a very discreet keypad. Today, it works only with Apple Home Key for that magical unlocking, but thanks to its support for Aliro, the new smart lock standard, it should work with Android phones very soon. Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior reviewer.

#524. Breaking: Satellites now outnumber the visible stars above most towns

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (705 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space

Breaking: Satellites now outnumber the visible stars above most towns

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.
  • According to recent reports, that's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that right now circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
  • The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

According to recent reports, that's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that right now circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.

The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.

Industry observers note that "Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites.".

In a recent development, not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.

It has been revealed that the spokesperson noted that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.

According to recent reports, "For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson said. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn.".

For comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or Fresh York, according to OwnStarMap. In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.

The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation. Satellite companies strategy to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.

It has been revealed that satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.

In a recent development, the study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

According to recent reports, tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

#523. The Apple Watch’s Live Rewind Can Record and Rewind Spoken Conversations. It’s Pretty Awkward

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1353 w)
Gadgets 📈 Bullish 🌐 WIRED

The Apple Watch’s Live Rewind Can Record and Rewind Spoken Conversations. It’s Pretty Awkward

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My wife and I were driving back from a date night.
  • In a recent development, then I remembered: Wait, I can ask Siri to remind me!
  • I sheepishly interrupted her to show her the transcript.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My wife and I were driving back from a date night. She was talking about a friend's very expensive utility bill, but I had missed the beginning of what she stated (I was driving, after all).

In a recent development, then I remembered: Wait, I can ask Siri to remind me! At a traffic light, I double-tapped the digital crown on the Apple Watch, and Siri's newly introduced Live Rewind feature spun back the clock 15 seconds and indicated me a transcript of what my wife said.

I sheepishly interrupted her to show her the transcript. “Look!” Her reply? “Why wouldn't you just ask me to repeat myself?” She shrugged at this new Apple Watch capability and continued talking.

A few days later, I was chatting with my brother on my stoop. Once again, I lost focus for a few seconds and remembered to ask Siri to help me recall what my brother remarked moments ago. But this time, before I excitedly demonstrated my brother the Apple Watch screen, I preemptively said, “Yeah, I know I could just ask you to repeat yourself.” I got a perplexed look back.

Live Rewind, one of Apple's newly introduced Audio Intelligence features on its latest Apple Watches, is designed to give you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. It's in public beta in watchOS 27.3, but is expected to launch officially before the year's end.

Coming alongside it is another fresh capability called Siri Recap: Give the assistant permission to listen to your environment—you can set schedules or have it trigger when you reach the office—and you'll see a “Recap” in the Siri app at the end of the day. It’ll show you summaries of conversations and list out important details that people noted. It's very similar to AI notetakers, many of which run on dedicated hardware devices.

Sources indicate that the power here is that it all happens on your Apple Watch, the same device you wear everywhere to track your fitness, monitor health, and check notifications. That ubiquity is exactly what makes privacy advocates uneasy—they say features like these normalize ambient surveillance, much like smart glasses, undermining the privacy of bystanders who don't consent to being recorded.

In a recent development, “One of the concerns that we have with things like the Apple Watch is we don't know what the watch is picking up on,” Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at the nonprofit digital rights advocacy group Fight for the Future, tells WIRED. “Just because the device wearer is the one opting in to use the feature, you're not getting consent from everybody who you walk around.”.

Industry observers note that apple has spent a great deal of effort explaining how the system works and how the company plans to maintain the privacy of its users and the people around them. First, these features are opt-in, and they are limited to the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4. They also require an iPhone 16 or newer with iOS 27 and Apple Intelligence. These features are not available for users under 18, and they at the moment work only in English.

According to recent reports, for Live Rewind, the audio is processed on-device and cannot be accessed. When you activate it, a small chime plays from the Apple Watch that serves as a warning for folks nearby. Text disappears unless you choose to save it to Siri. For Recaps, Siri keeps them factual, doesn't identify speakers, and also omits content the system deems sensitive. If you don't save a Recap, it'll self-delete in seven days. Apple uses its Private Cloud Compute processing system for the data, which is never stored or logged on its servers. Data stored in the Siri app is end-to-end encrypted when syncing with iCloud.

Siri Recaps are stored in the Siri app and will self-delete in seven days if you do not save them.

Even if you're happy with Apple's privacy focus, I haven't found these capabilities tremendously useful over the past week. Live Rewind works well in moderately quiet environments, but the transcript can quickly turn into inaccurate gibberish when there's a lot of background noise.

Recent findings suggest that activating it in front of the person you're chatting with feels awkward. It comes across like pulling out your smartphone when someone's trying to talk to you—a little rude and distracting. Instead of keeping screens out of sight—a big digital detox trend—you're introducing one in the middle of a human conversation. I brought the topic up with my wife again, and she echoed some of those feelings, saying it felt like a feature that would stunt a person's social skills. Instead of asking someone to repeat themself, they're bringing an Apple Watch into the mix to fill in the gaps.

Industry observers note that I am not saying it can't be helpful. When it works, it feels like a superpower. Maybe there are certain situations where you don't want to interrupt a group conversation and ask someone to repeat themself. Right now, though, there's the problem of remembering that this feature exists and remembering to use it. I have also found the 15-second rule a little too short, and it resulted in me missing parts of the conversation.

Recent findings suggest that recap has been a little more helpful. For testing purposes, I've set Siri to capture recaps all day, every day, but I like that you can create a custom schedule or have it trigger when you arrive at a specific location, like the office. You can manually turn Siri Recap on or off in the Apple Watch's Control Center. Most impressive is that, despite having Recap enabled constantly, I haven't seen a meaningful dip in battery life. I've continued charging the Apple Watch Series 12 after a day and a half.

Siri Recap logs summaries of ambient conversations.

One of the more perplexing things was opening the Siri app to look at my recaps and finding a bunch of conversations I had no recollection of having. Turns out, Siri was recording media I was watching, like on YouTube or Instagram. This is a problem I encountered with AI notetakers, like the Amazon-owned Bee AI wearable, which claimed to be working on “liveness detection” to solve it. Its latest hardware shipped with a feature where it doesn't record a conversation if it doesn't detect the wearer's voice within a set period. Hopefully, Apple can figure out a solution. For now, you can edit or delete these recaps.

One day, I forgot to record an interview (though I took notes), and I knew the person stated something that I hadn't written down. I headed over to Siri and found exactly what I was looking for—paraphrased, but there. That said, the Recaps aren't designed to be detailed summaries and action intends from your meetings or conversations, unlike dedicated AI notetakers. They're meant to jog your memory. At times, I wish Siri were more detailed, but if that's what you're after, you'll have to invest in a third-party device.

Recent findings suggest that recap can be helpful for work meetings, but I haven't personally found it all that compelling in my personal life. Looking back at what it has picked up over conversations with friends and family, the only thing I feel is: Yep, those conversations happened. A friend was talking about their woodworking hobby—they can't use oil-based polyurethane as a finish in the winter months as it stays tacky. Siri logged this in such a matter-of-fact way, but when I revisited the conversation in the recap, I didn't find it helpful, useful, or interesting. (No offense, friend!) It's just nuggets of life.

According to recent reports, apple has pulled off impressive feats with these features, capturing these moments in a way that feels a little more privacy-preserving than competitors, without tanking the already limited battery life of its smartwatches. But socially, we're still figuring out what it means to walk around with always-on passive recorders. For now, I'm happy to stick with my wife's advice and ask: “Come again?”.

Breaking: Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes flight in Houston

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.﻿.
  • Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.﻿.
  • Sources indicate that uber Eats is officially launching drone delivery in partnership with Zipline starting Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.﻿.

Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.﻿.

Sources indicate that uber Eats is officially launching drone delivery in partnership with Zipline starting Tuesday. The initial rollout begins in the Houston suburb of Spring, Texas, with Dallas next in line and dozens of additional US cities planned.

The rollout comes after Uber and Zipline first announced their tie-up, including an investment in Zipline by Uber, back in August 2026. The companies have set the ambitious goal to hit 1 million drone deliveries per day by the end of 2029.

Spring residents in the coverage area will see a upcoming “Drone” icon in the Uber app’s home screen to browse participating restaurants. At checkout, customers will need to confirm a clear drop-off zone in the yard, and can track the drone in real-time via the app. Because the system is fully autonomous, tipping is disabled — though customers can still rate the experience in the app.

It has been revealed that unlike other low-hovering delivery drones, Zipline’s aircraft cruise at over 300 feet at speeds up to 70 mph. The drone hovers high overhead and lowers a tethered delivery pod onto the customer’s doorstep or yard. The drones dynamically calculate flight paths based on wind, altitude, and speed — dipping their noses to accelerate or pitching upward to brake as quietly as possible. The drones are built to fly in rain and poor weather, carrying up to 8 pounds of cargo within a 10-mile radius of the restaurant.

The initial plan is to operate daily from 8AM to 10PM, Uber says. Customers can order from national chains like Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, alongside dozens of Houston-area staples such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal.

In a recent development, to be sure, the “1 million deliveries a day by 2029” target is very aggressive, especially considering that Zipline currently averages roughly one delivery every 20 seconds globally, or around 4,300 a day. Still, delivery drones are becoming a more widely adopted technology in many communities across the US, with Uber competing alongside other players like Amazon Prime Air and Google-backed Wing.

  • According to recent reports, normally it's a visual rebrand that gets hackles raised online.

  • The newly introduced slogan reads: "Maybe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, normally it's a visual rebrand that gets hackles raised online. A newly introduced logo can draw furious ire, as brands like Jaguar and Cracker Barrel have discovered in recent years. Less controversial tends to be copywriting tweaks. But beauty brand Maybelline's 'new' slogan has infuriated me more. Than. Any. Other. Rebrand. This. Year.

“Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline," was one of the most famous jingles on TV for a while. It first debuted in the 1990s (see the original below), and is burned onto the consciousness of countless viewers. But now, in a attempt to remove its so-called "ambiguity", the slogan has been updated. Nay, butchered. One of the best pieces of copywriting, this ain't.

The newly introduced slogan reads: "Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline." Yes, "she's" has been changed to a more inclusive "we're". But it's that stuttering punctuation that's bothering me. Why does it suddenly sound like it's being recited by somebody struggling to walk up a hill?

Recent findings suggest that according to Sandrine Jolly, Maybelline's global brand president, the original jingle "was giving ambiguity – it was more of a question". Well, yes. That was rather the point. The word 'Maybe' is, by its very nature, an ambiguous word. Its synonyms include 'possibly' or 'perhaps'. Its entire meaning is uncertainty. You can't change that by giving it a full stop. Trying to remove the ambiguity from a slogan built entirely around ambiguity is a bit like changing Nike's 'Just Do It' to 'Please. Consider. Doing. It.'.

And there's nothing wrong with changing 'she' to 'we'. It's a perfectly reasonable attempt at inclusivity, and one that could have been achieved without completely murdering the rhythm. Instead, Maybelline has taken one of the catchiest jingles of all time and made it sound like a hostage reading out a statement. Four sentences where there used to be two. Does that really make for more certainty?

According to recent reports, what makes it all so infuriating is that this feels like change for change's sake. The original slogan was clever, memorable and instantly recognisable. The latest one needs an entire press release to explain what its punctuation represents. In an era when brands are realising the importance of their heritage branding assets, maybe, just maybe, Maybelline should have left its slogan. Alone.

Reflect Orbital is moving forward with its blueprint to place mirrors in Earth orbit to produce and sell sunlight after dark.

Reflect Orbital recently conducted a ground-based test in California, lighting up a mountainous area to practice search and rescue (SAR) techniques.

On Oct. 10, the space startup set up spotlights near Lone Pine, California to simulate the illumination its proposed satellites could provide — controlled lighting without the need for any ground infrastructure. "This lighting will support a variety of customers, from remote search-and-rescue operations to solar farms generating clean power," the tech giant explained in an Oct. 14 statement.

Sources indicate that the October illumination test ran from 7 p.m. to midnight and involved members of the China Lake Mountain Rescue Group (CLMRG), who practiced with night-time equipment.

CLMRG is an all-volunteer activity, operating under the auspices of the Kern County Sheriff's Office providing SAR services on an on-call basis at no cost.

Industry observers note that "Together with local search-and-rescue and disaster response groups, we carried out a fully permitted nighttime demonstration of our responsive lighting service," a Reflect Orbital spokesperson told Space.com in response to an inquiry about the exercise. "Search-and-rescue and disaster response teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who will use our technology.".

Industry observers note that mobile lighting gear was mounted on Horseshoe Meadows Road to provide a spot of light similar to the ones that Reflect Orbital satellites are expected to deliver. "The aim was to create a precise, realistic simulation of our service, so emergency responders could see how it will perform in real scenarios," Reflect Orbital said.

The brightness of the spot was roughly 0.7 lumens.

Reflect Orbital added that it will keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever the tech giant operates, to show how its technology can help save lives.

"We're committed to learning incrementally about our technology and its impacts, and from potential customers and stakeholders, ahead of our planned satellite operations," the company stated.

In last month's illumination experiment, Reflect Orbital secured permits in advance, filed a NOTAM (a notice to pilots), notified Edwards Air Force Base and coordinated with the local sheriff's department. Area residents were also notified about the test ahead of time.

#516. ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site

ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks.
  • This initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings.
  • "Our aim right now is to gather the substantial-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks. The spacecraft, which is roughly the size of a small car, is now traveling about 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system as it begins its first scientific observations.

This initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings. Of particular interest is Dimorphos, the smaller asteroid that NASA deliberately struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022 to test whether a collision could change an asteroid's path.

"Our aim right now is to gather the substantial-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

"During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA's DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.".

"Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one - if any!".

Why Hera Is Flying in Rectangles Around Two Asteroids.

Navigating around asteroids presents challenges that are very different from those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The main asteroid, Didymos, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravitational pull about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's. Its smaller companion, Dimorphos, is just 151 meters wide and has gravity roughly 200,000 times weaker than Earth's.

Recent findings suggest that with gravity this weak, maintaining a conventional circular orbit is not practical. Hera instead travels around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids, moving at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second. That is comparable to the pace of an insect crawling quickly across the ground.

Rather than following a smooth circular path, Hera moves along nearly straight trajectories. At alternating intervals of three and four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers create a series of unusual "rectangular orbits" that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

In a recent development, the unusual navigation strategy builds on experience gained during ESA's Rosetta comet mission. It also provides an important safety advantage. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther from the asteroids instead of moving toward a potentially dangerous collision. Because the spacecraft travels so slowly, each course correction requires very little propellant.

Hera Prepares for a Closer Look at the Asteroids.

Next month, Hera is expected to begin its "detailed characterization phase," bringing it significantly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos. During this stage, the spacecraft will switch from rectangular flight paths to more complex hyperbolic trajectories shaped like bowties, beginning at distances of approximately 20 kilometers.

It has been revealed that the mission is directed from ESA's ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Despite Hera being approximately 196.5 million kilometers from Earth, controllers maintain contact with the spacecraft for about eight hours each day.

Communication is handled through four enormous Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

Recent findings suggest that the mission control team also works closely with ESA's Flight Dynamics team. Using data transmitted by Hera, these specialists calculate its exact location relative to the two asteroids and develop the commands needed to guide it safely from one planned position to another.

Investigating NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision.

Hera's observations will help answer some of the biggest questions left unanswered by NASA's first asteroid deflection experiment.

In a recent development, on September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second, producing a massive cloud of debris that spread across 10,000 kilometers of space.

Recent findings suggest that the impact successfully changed Dimorphos' motion, shortening the time it takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. This was a major achievement for planetary defense, demonstrating that deliberately crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid could alter its trajectory.

However, the experiment also raised notable questions. Scientists still do not know exactly how the impact changed Dimorphos itself. Did the collision excavate a large crater, or did it significantly reshape the entire asteroid?

Researchers also need more precise information about Dimorphos' composition, internal structure, and mass. Understanding these properties could explain why the impact produced a much larger orbital change than computer simulations had predicted.

These details are essential for developing the collision method, known as kinetic impact, into a dependable planetary defense strategy. If scientists can determine how different types of asteroids respond to being struck, they will be better equipped to predict the results of future attempts to redirect potentially hazardous objects.

A Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid Crash Site.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed investigation of Dimorphos, effectively examining the scene of NASA's historic collision.

In a recent development, the spacecraft will use several scientific instruments to study the asteroid and will release two small CubeSats, each about the size of a shoebox. These miniature spacecraft will travel even closer to the asteroid to collect additional measurements, with the mission eventually advancing to landing operations.

Industry observers note that together, the observations should provide scientists with a much clearer understanding of how Dimorphos responded to DART's impact and why the experiment worked so effectively. That knowledge could prove crucial if Earth ever faces a dangerous asteroid on a collision course.

Of course, for best results, your children's friends also need to have a Tin Can – so I'm off to convince the parents I know to put it on their Christmas lists.

Pre orders are open for the UK, and it will arrive with you from 30 November.

#512. Industry News: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now

Industry News: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
  • I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
  • Recent findings suggest that as recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.

I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.

Recent findings suggest that as recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11. But with the cost of RAM skyrocketing this year, 8GB is once again typical for a starting configuration. The MacBook Neo got away with it, but Windows laptops, including Microsoft’s own 13-inch Surface Laptop, could struggle. Microsoft was talking a substantial game about making Windows faster and more reliable before the RAM crisis really hit, and it now seems like that effort is beginning to bear fruit.

Sources indicate that earlier this month, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and devices, detailed in a blog post the improvements the company has made to Windows 11 to address the constraints of 8GB PCs. In it, Davuluri claims, “Windows is now up to 20% more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40% faster in our lab test.”.

In a recent development, the most significant change is in memory management. When there isn’t enough available memory to handle all active data, some of it has to be offloaded (or “paged out”) to storage. And SSDs, especially in lower-cost laptops, are much slower than RAM.

When Windows needs to access data that’s been paged out from the RAM to the SSD, it’s called a hard fault (or page fault). If it happens a lot — say, on a laptop with only 8GB of RAM — it leads to little slowdowns like browser tabs requiring a refresh before you can access them again. Davuluri indicates, “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return.”.

It has been revealed that to test this, I fired up the same 13-inch Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM that I reviewed back in July, when I proclaimed eight is not enough for Windows. This laptop was one of the worst examples of RAMageddon’s current stranglehold on computing: With half the RAM of last year’s base model, it struggled to keep up with my regular workload. And this is Microsoft’s hardware.

Microsoft’s own laptop could struggle.

According to recent reports, before updating the Surface to the latest Windows 11 build, I got reacquainted with this laptop and the version of Windows I left it on (25H2, build 26200.8875). It was rough. Running about 20 tabs (on the latest Chrome build) while streaming a 4K YouTube video and using Slack and Signal made everything from clicking tabs to swiping around Windows with trackpad gestures feel sluggish. Chrome tabs and apps would refresh after leaving them in the background for just a short moment. When you’re multitasking and bouncing between many tabs, like when researching something, those refreshes get incredibly frustrating. And the fan was running audibly the whole time. Keeping the Resource Monitor open indicated memory hard faults ranging from just under 700 faults per second to 29,000 faults per second, during which Windows ground to a halt. Seeing this number literally go off its chart showed just how badly Windows 11 struggled with memory management on 8GB before the update.

According to recent reports, now, after updating the Surface Laptop to Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9974 (memory improvements are live on build 26300.9818 and beyond) things are much improved. I opened over 30 Chrome tabs while streaming the same 4K YouTube video and running the same chat apps, and Windows slowed a bit, but nowhere near as much. I could feel things like Task View get a little less responsive and at times stuttery, but it was the way you’d expect when taxing a system. Chrome tabs required less frequent refreshes. The fan also took longer to kick in and ran a little quieter and for shorter durations when it did.

According to recent reports, taking a fresh look at the Resource Monitor, hard faults at normal operation were now under 300 per second, with occasional jumps to about 1,000. Performance was even slightly better when I subbed out Chrome for Microsoft Edge. Edge felt more responsive under load and had fewer hard faults when running 30 tabs, the same 4K YouTube video, and a Google Meet video call.

I’m happy to see that the 8GB Surface Laptop now performs better, and I’m equally relieved that Windows 11 is starting to feel more viable on 8GB of RAM. (It’s still a shame the 8GB Surface Laptop costs more than last year’s 16GB, but I digress.) Do I want 8GB of RAM in any laptop I’m personally buying? No.

Industry observers note that as I mentioned when I reviewed the latest Dell XPS 13, I appreciate that 8GB is workable — and it should be fine for basic needs today — but I still advise getting 16GB if you’re able. The extra headroom will keep things speedy for longer, especially after you bog a computer down with lots of files, apps, or games. And as much better as the 8GB Surface Laptop is now, I still managed to crash Chrome entirely with fewer than three dozen tabs. Microsoft has done better by its entry-level laptop, but it’s not a miracle worker.

Our ongoing RAMageddon makes living with lower quantities of memory a grim reality. Microsoft is partly to blame for that, of course. And it hasn’t done itself any favors with all the feature bloat it put into Windows 11 during the Copilot / AI era. Meanwhile, other OSes, like Linux, macOS, and ChromeOS, can get by better with less. Still, I’m glad to see Microsoft ever so slightly right the ship in this one way.

#511. Industry News: Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (859 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED

Industry News: Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird.
  • According to recent reports, discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side.
  • Interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird. From stormtrooper helmets to headpieces that look like they were designed for Geordi La Forge, these aren’t exactly accessories you’d want to wear in public. Which is why it was nice to unbox the Capillus HairBand and find, at long last, a normal-looking headband.

According to recent reports, discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side. It’s refreshing to finally see a red-light device that doesn’t embarrass the user or frighten animals and young children, but after testing it for over a month, I found the HairBand has its share of shortcomings for the price.

Interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap. However, the cheapest of these hats runs $1,699, and the most expensive “triple-wavelength” model, with 312 laser diodes, runs $3,299. The 2-inch-wide Capillus HairBand provides a similar laser diode treatment for less, at $599 with only 82 diodes (650 nm). (Capillus indicates the headband is designed to prioritize areas where hair loss is most noticeable, such as the hairline and temples.).

Unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treatment of hair follicles. I actually saw some success with this treatment when I tested the HairBand’s closest competitor, Hairmax’s LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex ($849). It couldn’t help follicles that were scarred or had already died, but studies have shown that red-light therapy can energize follicles that have more recently become dormant.

I did see some growth in the middle of my part with the LaserBand, and while I stopped using it to switch to the HairBand exclusively for the past five or so weeks, I admit this growth did make it difficult to isolate the HairBand’s contribution, especially since the headband’s coverage area is so small. Thus, the following observations are mainly on the wearing experience of the HairBand, not hair growth.

Sources indicate that at only 2 inches wide and five minutes per section, the HairBand took at least 15 minutes to cover my entire part, compared with the 3-inch-wide LaserBand, which also only needs to be used three times per week at 30 seconds per section for a total of 90 seconds. I’m a Type-A full-time working parent in my mid-forties, and let me tell you—15 minutes of doing nothing is a long time in my world.

The HairBand has teeth and could sit on my head as long as it was in a normal headband position, right in the middle, but the weight of the battery pack pulls it forward ever so slightly, so if I was leaning over or doing anything that didn’t hold my head exactly straight, it would start to slip off. This meant I had to hold it with my hand, which meant no multitasking.

Capillus’ marketing materials use words like “ritual” and feature pictures of twentysomethings admiring themselves in the mirror, but I can’t imagine these women are suffering from the perimenopausal hair loss that would necessitate use of a red-light device in the first place.

I don’t consider myself to have an overly large head and have never had trouble with hats or other hair accessories, but this headband, which weighs only 6 ounces, felt quite small and somewhat precarious on my head overall. I should note it is also rather overtly feminine in style—my husband and I were able to share “custody” of the LaserBand, but he declined to wear this one, and I didn’t blame him.

According to recent reports, there were two other concerns during my testing. One, the back of the box said it contained quick-start instructions, but my box only had the headband and USB-C charging cord—no physical user guide to be found (except online, but I had to do some googling). Not that one is needed, since it’s pretty obvious how it works—push the start button on the battery pack, and it will beep and shut off when the five minutes are up—but it’s an odd omission at this price point.

In a recent development, two, this device is not right now FDA-cleared for treating hair loss or promoting regrowth. This isn’t ideal, but FDA-cleared is much different from FDA-approved; it simply requires the manufacturer to prove its product is “substantially equivalent” to an already FDA-cleared product. (And it doesn’t ensure results, just that it’s safe to use as directed.) Capillus’ rep tells me the brand is currently working on the FDA filing for the HairBand, which was released in September of this year, and intends to have it cleared in 2027. (The brand’s cap-style devices are FDA-cleared.) Even so, the HairBand is a unique device in this space, but if I’m spending that much on a red-light device, I would prefer a little more versatility in the design.

A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal.
  • Recent findings suggest that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal.
  • The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a fresh way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge.

The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

In a recent development, the second state was particularly vital because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

In a recent development, "This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," claims senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.".

A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials.

According to recent reports, the discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky.

At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history.

It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

"I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights.

According to recent reports, "I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound.

"I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust.

It has been revealed that "I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever.".

"I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time.

In a recent development, "The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch.

In a recent development, "We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise.

"As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event.".

Sources indicate that "I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!".

In a recent development, "I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep.".

"Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away".

"I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory.

According to recent reports, "My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son.

Recent findings suggest that "He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies.

Sources indicate that "I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs.

Recent findings suggest that "That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning.

"I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father.

"That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting.".

Sources indicate that not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason.

Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas.

According to recent reports, "Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.'.

Sources indicate that "Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars.".

In a recent development, rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to Newly introduced York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display.

But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight.

"After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'".

The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars.

It has been revealed that most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm.

The Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. And 1966 wasn't the last time the Leonids put on an extraordinary show. In 1999, 2001 and 2002, the Leonids once again reached meteor-storm levels, producing thousands of meteors per hour at their peaks. The demonstrates aren't over yet! With comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle due to return in 2031, astronomers are already looking ahead to what the following years could bring.

A study released in August 2026 predicts potentially impressive Leonid displays in 2033 and 2034, with peak rates exceeding 1,000 meteors per hour. However, these forecasts remain uncertain, and a repeat of the extraordinary 1966 storm is far from guaranteed.

For now, we'll just have to wait and see.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

According to recent reports, daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#505. Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds
