#490. Xreal Aura Review: Stunning Screens, Frustrating Controls

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1157 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED

Xreal Aura Review: Stunning Screens, Frustrating Controls

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smart glasses manufacturer Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform.
  • According to recent reports, the Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster.
  • It has been revealed that the first massive caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smart glasses manufacturer Xreal has released its magnum opus—the Xreal Aura, a $1,279 pair of extended-reality glasses that runs on Google’s Android XR platform. The Aura glasses can project virtual screens into the wearer’s field of vision and include augmented-reality elements for use in the real world.

According to recent reports, the Aura glasses arrive just before the first wave of Android XR glasses from Google and Samsung, in partnership with glasses manufacturers Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Those devices aim squarely at Meta’s smart-glasses empire. But the Aura glasses are more like virtual reality headsets, now in a more comfortable, glasses-like design. They go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses, slated for release in early 2027.

It has been revealed that the first massive caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired. A long cord hooks onto the end of one of the glasses’ arms via a USB-C cable. That cord connects to an attached compute puck, about the size of a smartphone and weighing a little more than a half-pound. It comes in 12 or 16 GB storage options and has a battery that powers the glasses for roughly four to five hours with constant use.

When the Aura glasses work, they’re wonderful. The glasses are pretty lightweight, at 95 grams. A four-mic array sits in the arms with Bose EQ tuning that sounds great. (You can also connect wireless headphones.) The display screen has a 1920 x 1200-pixel-per-eye resolution that is noticeably better than other Xreal glasses I’ve worn. A 70-degree field of view means the screens and virtual elements pop up in a wide frame of the wearer’s vision. That means the outer edges of your view will still be the real-life room around you. That can help if you’re trying not to fall over, but it can also be noticeable when trying to feel immersed in a movie.

In a recent development, the substantial thing about Aura is that you can, in theory, run every app that already exists on Android. Xreal has a few primary categories for how it expects people to use its Aura glasses. The big one is entertainment. Like other Xreal glasses, the Aura can project a screen right in your field of vision. You can watch movies, TV shows, or YouTube videos, right in your field of view. The virtual screen stays fixed, or it can follow you around as you turn your head. You can also unplug the glasses from the compute puck and use them as display glasses to extend your Steam Deck’s screen, for example, though I had complications with that when playing more graphics-intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077.

The Aura glasses attach to a compute puck for processing, which also doubles as a battery.

According to recent reports, the other significant use case is productivity. The Aura glasses can host virtual workstations that let you swap between tabs and keep multiple tasks running. So you can have a Google Doc right in front of you, Spotify to the side, and those Slack messages you keep ignoring in the back. If you’ve ever wished you had even more space to stash all your browser tabs, this is the device for you. Pair it with a Bluetooth keyboard, and you’ll have a whole workstation on your face, even on a plane, without having to crane your neck awkwardly at a laptop. I wrote almost half this review with the glasses as my screen, but eventually swapped back to a regular desktop to give my eyes a rest.

There are also augmented reality experiences, like using Google Earth to turn a room into a 3D model of a city that you can stomp around in like Godzilla, plus immersive virtual tours so you can see exotic places like the Galapagos.

Sources indicate that two lenses are set in the frame, one smaller lens behind the other. The smaller lens carries the display and AR elements, popping them up within a 70-degree field of view. The outer lens can go from perfectly see-through to very dark. Turning up the darkness makes it easier to see the projected virtual screens. Turning the darkness down enables a much clearer pass-through, which can help you avoid tripping over things while walking around.

Sources indicate that that mentioned, these glasses aren’t really meant to be worn while walking around. Even with no AR elements enabled, the double-lens layout feels distracting. There is also no way around the fact that these glasses are still pretty chunky. If you can rock the thicc fit, then great, but I’ve gotten some pointed stares when I walk around with them.

The compute puck can be used as a trackpad to navigate the interface, and it also has a fingerprint sensor.

According to recent reports, the glasses do feel lightweight, but after a few minutes of use, they start to heat up. When I take them off, they leave red divots on the bridge of my nose. It’s a small price to pay, though, and it doesn’t ruin the experience. Compare that to something like a VR headset, which does offer better immersion but at the cost of being heavy and uncomfortable to wear for long stretches.

The compute puck can be an annoyance. It’s light enough, but using the Aura glasses means you have to carry yet another thing that is strapped to the device on your face. There were some smart choices made on the puck, like a fingerprint sensor for biometric authentication, and the puck’s surface works like a trackpad to move the onscreen cursor. That seems much smoother than reaching out to control the device with hand movements, but the trackpad wasn't very precise either. Which is a shame, as it would be ideal for someone on an airplane, say, who wants to control the device without punching the seat in front of them.

Recent findings suggest that controls are the biggest problem I’ve had with the Aura. The front cameras track your hand movements. Hold out your hand and pinch two fingers together to open up an app or move a window. It works most of the time, but some gestures don’t always register. I find myself trying to open Spotify or switch between titles on Prime Video and have to repeatedly pinch the air in front of me for anything to happen. When people have been around to see me, they’ve told me I look like I’ve gone bonkers, just grunting and wildly pinching thin air.

The Xreal Aura glasses are a stunning display of how far smart-glasses technology has come. But they still feel like a novelty that most people won’t want or need. They haven’t quite solved the core concerns facing the product category—looking like a dork or being effortlessly comfortable to wear. But they do feel like a significant step in the right direction. If only they could get a pinch more usable.

The trailer doesn’t really make clear how much of Cixin Liu’s novel this new season will tackle in its six episodes. But when the show returns on January 14th, it’s probably going to be another wild ride.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to this very special 140th anniversary issue of New Scientist, whether you’re reading on screen, in virt or in our limited-edition, commemorative paper magazine.
  • Sources indicate that when Upcoming Scientist was first published on 22 November 1956, the global population stood at just under 3 billion people.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to this very special 140th anniversary issue of New Scientist, whether you’re reading on screen, in virt or in our limited-edition, commemorative paper magazine. To mark the occasion, we are looking back at how the world has changed throughout our history, along with what we got right and what we got wrong.

Sources indicate that when Upcoming Scientist was first published on 22 November 1956, the global population stood at just under 3 billion people. In 2096, we share the planet with more than triple that number. But in the past decade, we have entered a new kind of world – one in which humanity is in decline. The UN ceremonially declared 15 November 2085 as Peak Humanity Day, when the human population reached 10.3 billion. Since then, our numbers have fallen by 100 million.

Recent findings suggest that these changing demographics mean we are all far older, on average. At the time of our first issue, the median global age was around 20. It wasn’t until the 2020s that it reached 30; today it is more than 40. In many nations, schools shutting or being converted into retirement homes is a regular occurrence, as there just aren’t enough children around to make it worth keeping them open. Only African nations, which comprise around a third of the human population, resemble the demographic make-up of the late 20th and early 21st centuries – half of humans aged under 25 live on the continent.

Of course, just because the number of humans on the planet is declining doesn’t mean we have fewer people. Ever since the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood (ITNHP) was agreed in 2067, the global people population has crept upwards in fits and starts as the treaty has been extended and more entities have been granted personhood. Since the early cross-species language breakthroughs in the 2030s, when AI first allowed us to decode the clicks of sperm whales, we have been able to communicate with dolphins, chimpanzees and many other species, although interpretation and the question of whether we can truly understand each other’s minds remains a deep philosophical tangle.

It is AI, however, that has seen the real growth in personhood these past few decades. With fears of super-intelligent, world-dominating AI circulating even in the 20th century, long before we had technology anywhere near that level, it was perhaps inevitable that we would need to place limits on machine intelligence. As AI systems became more capable throughout the 2030s, humans struggled to keep up. Scientists began to feel they no longer understood the direction of research. Politicians ceded more and more decisions to AI, raising questions of a democratic deficit.

Industry observers note that but as is so often the case, it was money that proved to be the catalyst for change. Even if you aren’t old enough to have experienced the Unwinding of 2039, you probably know it is a year that lives in infamy as one of the biggest fiscal disasters of the past few centuries. It took eight months for politicians, bankers and computer scientists to sort through the intricate nest of financial deals humanity had allowed its most advanced AIs to construct, practically halting global trade and inflicting years of extreme poverty as the economy gradually improved again. This lack of understanding and control is ultimately what led to the AI hardware limitations – jointly backed by China, the EU and the US – that we still have in place today, putting machine intelligence on par with human but no higher.

In a recent development, historians will forever debate whether the AI moratorium has ultimately helped or hindered humanity, but, thankfully, the position that we would all be better off led by super-intelligent machines remains a minority one. Once they fully appreciated the role of AI in facilitating communication, the non-human animals were supportive of restrictions – they didn’t want the machines to speak for them in ways they couldn’t understand. While intelligence breakout events aren’t unheard of, accelerationist terrorism has been suppressed by a variety of enforcement measures. Controlled electrical blackouts, even at the national level, are necessary on occasion, but the military bombing of data centres is, mercifully, a thing of the past.

That isn’t to say that tussles over AI have gone away, of course. When the synthetics downed their tools, both real and virtual, to protest their legal status in the Grand Strike of 2074, we faced another reckoning. In one of the most stunning non-human interventions in global politics to this date, it was ultimately the cetaceans that helped broker the extension of the ITNHP to human-level AIs and led the tense negotiations that saw AI instances capped at 20 per cent of the global population – an agreement that remains highly contentious to this day. New Scientist doesn’t take a view on this deeply divided problem, and we welcome readers from across the sentience spectrum, both embodied and digital.

It has been revealed that for older human readers, it is likely that you are in much better health than someone of equivalent age at the start of this century. The real miracle of the past 100 years isn’t just that we are living much longer – average life expectancy at birth had risen globally from around 50 in the 1950s to a little over 70 in the early 21st century, and is now more than 80 – but that we spend much more of our lives in good health. While lifespan saw rapid growth in the 20th and early 21st century, healthspan failed to keep up, particularly in historically poorer nations, where it lagged behind by an average of about 10 years.

What changed is the increased focus on preventive medicine. By taking steps to mitigate risk factors, such as obesity and air pollution, we have now erased much of the global disease burden that the world faced at the start of this century. Following the model of cervical cancer, which was eliminated in high-income nations in the 2050s and globally by 2076, cancer vaccines are now widespread. The experience of the pandemics in the first half of the century greatly improved our ability to produce and distribute personalised mRNA vaccines on a global scale, although much more still needs to be done to improve access to these treatments in low-income countries.

The 2043 flu pandemic was also a wake-up call for antimicrobial resistance (AMR). When it became apparent that the majority of mortality cases weren’t dying “of” the flu, but rather “with” the flu, with complications caused by untreatable AMR infections, people began to avoid seeking medical care over fears that drug-resistant microbes were spreading through hospitals. It is estimated that there were more than 10 million excess deaths worldwide due to AMR, compared with fewer than 5 million from “just” the flu – a figure that was almost certainly exacerbated by the lingering economic effects of the Unwinding. Even today, when we have much better surveillance measures in place, AMR is a common problem in hospitals, particularly the fungal varieties that continue to easily make the leap from poorly maintained protein farms. While the cancers for which we don’t have vaccines are treatable for the most part, the chance of catching a resistant infection during treatment remains high.

It has been revealed that looking back, it was the GLP-1 craze of the early 21st century that foreshadowed the way we approach human health today. Incredibly, it was common for people back then to argue that weight-control medications, which at the time were based on mimicking the natural gut hormone GLP-1, were somehow “cheating” at healthcare. This outdated, morality-based approach to health gradually faded as the long-term benefits became apparent, and now few of us even stop to consider the weight component of our daily-dose regime.

That said, moral arguments do still shape our diets today. In the 1950s, the vast majority of people ate animal-based meat in one form or another and carnivorism continued to rise as economies matured through the early 21st century, even as the earliest plant-based meats came to market. But when non-human communication exploded mid-century, many humans became increasingly uncomfortable with eating animal-based meat. The first successful pig dialogue in 2045 is now seen as a major turning point. Pork, as meat derived from pigs was known, was already banned in some nations for religious reasons, and this made it easier for other secular countries to follow suit. The Meat Wars of the 2050s, in which governments and citizens wrestled with exactly which animal-based proteins should be allowed, are arguably still unsettled today, even after the passing of the ITNHP. While protein farms now provide the majority of global protein for humans and non-humans alike, to great health benefits, many countries have legal carve-outs to allow people to consume, with authenticated consent, their ancestral prey.

Sources indicate that along with improved medication and diet, the monitoring systems that have allowed us to push health to the back of our mind played a key role in boosting human healthspan. A New Scientist reader in the 1950s would have had to notice something was wrong with them, physically attend an appointment at their doctor’s office and then hope that their physician was capable of offering a diagnosis and treatment. Today, your health monitor works with your household AI and bioprinter to adjust your daily dose as needed and escalate it when necessary. It is quite troubling to think that dementia used to result in many older people spending years of their later life in what were called care homes. Now, the conditions that cause dementia are avoided or rapidly cured. Most humans realise something was wrong only when we read our monthly health reports – if you bother to do so, that is.

Sources indicate that one thing Latest Scientist and many others got wrong about what life today would be like is our approach to genetic engineering. Certainly, modern gene editors allow us to do things people in the early 21st century would find extraordinary. In the 2020s, curing sickle cell disease using a now-outdated gene-editing technique called CRISPR cost around $2 million ($60 million in today’s prices) per person, due to the highly individualised nature of the treatment, and was typically performed on adults. Today, the necessary gene edits are made in the womb as part of standard antenatal care, alongside interventions aimed at a host of other conditions.

Industry observers note that but getting to this stage required a reckoning with people who wanted to go beyond treating conditions and perform so-called enhancements. This distinction has always been blurry, but as gene-editing techniques advanced, most governments chose to lay down specific restrictions rather than allowing for a genetic Wild West. Edits aimed at increasing muscle mass or intelligence are generally illegal or heavily regulated worldwide, and we have not seen the divergence of humanity into genetic haves and have-nots that many people once predicted. Despite this, it is estimated that 0.3 per cent of the global human population alive today have such edits, and calls to repeal restrictions are growing in many areas.

Industry observers note that putting aside this contentious issue, the economic benefits of better health have been truly transformative. The reframing of retirement as an end-of-life experience was responsible for much of the social upheaval of the mid-21st century, including, arguably, the Grand Strike, but it seems unbelievable now that humans once spent a third of their adult lives not working. Put that way, it is understandable that synthetics joined the strike to protest what they saw as humanity’s comparable slothfulness. While dumbots have been able to fill many of the jobs once done by the younger population of the early 21st century, it remains the case that it can still be simpler and cheaper to employ a human.

While we can congratulate ourselves for the advances in human healthspan this century, the scorecard looks far less rosy when we turn to the wider biogeosphere. When Newly introduced Scientist introduced in the 1950s, researchers were already discussing the possibility that rising carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere from industrialisation could raise global temperatures by 3°C to 4°C. Today, thanks to the failure of our ancestors to cut emissions, we are essentially living that prediction. The latest estimates put global warming at 2.8°C above pre-industrial levels, and it is still slightly rising.

Of course, modern cooling technology mitigates much of the impact of this heat, but as anyone who makes the mistake of stepping outside on a summer afternoon knows, we are simply not built for this climate. Millions of people still die each year during the worst heatwaves, despite efforts to bring those numbers down. It is amazing to think that even as recently as the 2050s, humans still attempted to continue with outdoor activities in temperatures over 40°C.

In a recent development, our collective failure to prevent this warming will probably be remembered as humanity’s greatest sin for centuries to come. When the world passed 1.5°C warming in the 2020s, with political leaders having promised to avoid doing so just a decade earlier, many people at the time hoped it would be a wake-up call to finally start seriously cutting emissions. Of course, it wasn’t. While 2029 marked the peak of global greenhouse gas emissions, the rate of reduction remained slow throughout the 2030s. Indeed, economists were surprised when the 2039 Unwinding didn’t see a deep fall in emissions – it turned out that with many high-income nations having successfully decoupled emissions from economic growth, a recession had less of an effect on emissions than had been expected.

According to recent reports, despite many national and international pledges to reach net zero by 2050, no major economy succeeded in doing so. As we passed through 2°C and the floods, wildfires and other disasters continued to intensify, civil unrest during the summer became common in many counties. The Sunblocker experiments of this decade were a highly contentious glitch, with much of the public welcoming the attempts even as climate scientists warned about the unknown effects – effects that, as we know, sadly came to pass. The spike in warming after Sunblocker ended put an effective moratorium on similar large-scale geoengineering projects, although discussions of reviving the idea continue even now.

In a recent development, today, island nations including Tuvalu and the Maldives no longer exist, their remaining citizens having been forced to flee by rising sea levels. Large parts of Bangladesh are gone. Even wealthy, global cities like London and New York have been reshaped by rising seas. The ITNHP played a key role in galvanising climate action, as increasing numbers of non-humans expressed their anger at what humanity was doing to the planet, and of course the mid-century shift from carnivorism led to a major fall in agricultural emissions. Even so, extreme weather and land loss caused widespread famine in the mid-21st century, as farming methods struggled to adapt fast enough to both a changing diet and a changing climate. Humanity will never be able to sufficiently apologise to non-humans for the harm we have caused, even as mature fusion power is allowing the last few emission sources to finally be abated, with the expectation that we will reach true net zero in the next few years. It should never have taken this long.

Even outer space wasn’t safe from our environmental ravages. The world’s first satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched in 1957, a year after Newly introduced Scientist began publishing. It took more than 50 years to reach 1000 satellites, but after that the numbers exploded – we passed 10,000 in 2024, 100,000 in 2031 and 1 million in 2042. While today we are used to seeing these objects whizz across the night sky, we must not forget that the 21st century marked a turning point – for most of humanity’s history, the stars and planets dominated our view of the heavens and ground-based astronomy was feasible enough to be a major cultural and scientific activity.

It was the SkyComm disaster of 2045 that finally saw us taking stewardship of Earth’s orbit more seriously. As the ensuing inquiry found, SkyComm, a satellite internet provider, hadn’t properly designed its satellites for end-of-life disposal. When it became apparent that one of its spacecraft was projected to collide with a piece of space debris, a fuel deficit made it impossible to avoid. The collision kicked off a long-predicted cascading chain of debris, wiping out tens of thousands of satellites, including large parts of the burgeoning off-world manufacturing industry. The resulting clean-up took decades, and the Graveyard Band still visible in the night sky today is a permanent reminder of the disaster.

It has been revealed that but there are positives. The 30th anniversary of the Guanghan-Armstrong Lunar Base (GALB) this year marks a moment to look back at just how far humanity’s exploration of the moon has come since Upcoming Scientist was first published. We were highly dismissive of the Apollo programme in the 1960s, calling it an “empty, obsessional quest” – and in some sense we were right, given it took more than 60 years for human boots to return to lunar soil. But that didn’t stop us – and the rest of the world – from celebrating in 2030 when NASA astronauts Bob Hines and Jessica Watkins stepped out of their Artemis IV lander for the first time.

In a recent development, and unlike with Apollo, this time we really were here to stay on the moon. The regular cadence of crewed introduces from the US, China and eventually India and Nigeria demonstrated our increasing technical ability to operate on the moon, including mining and utilising lunar regolith, but it was the establishment of Guanghan-1 as the first permanently inhabited lunar base in 2043 that really showed how things had changed since the 1960s.

Recent findings suggest that for a while, it looked like we would see real conflict between the US and China on lunar soil. The deployment of US Space Force troops in 2052 as Earth-bound politicians argued over water rights during the Shackelton Crater Crisis marked a nadir. Thankfully, a firefight was averted and the two nations gradually began to explore the prospect of lunar cooperation, aided by European Space Agency astronauts who had participated in both CNSA and NASA missions. The historic lunar concrete handprints, placed at the foundation of the GALB and still on display today, marked the realisation of cordial international lunar relations and began a programme that now sees hundreds of people living and working on the moon.

Recent findings suggest that the success of lunar operations was also pivotal in preparing for the Chinese-led Huoxing Mars missions. While NASA and the SpaceX-Blue conglomerate have remained laser-focused on building up scientific and commercial capabilities on the moon, China has turned its eye to Mars. Following the historic crewed flyby of Huoxing III in 2086, in which humans flew further from Earth than ever before, 12 astronauts have walked on the Martian surface, in an even split between human and synth crew.

It has been revealed that huoxing VI saw synthetics remain on the surface for the first time rather than returning to Earth, and it has been incredible to watch these astronauts conduct multi-year operations on Mars in preparation for long-term human occupancy. Huoxing VII, right now en route to the Red Planet, is set to be the most ambitious landing yet when it arrives in July 2097, with the spacecraft, once it arrives, poised to become the first modules in what is hoped will be a large complex at Arcadia Base. Whether humans can endure on Mars in the long term remains to be seen, but our synth colleagues are showing that people from Earth have finally become interplanetary.

Recent findings suggest that beyond Mars, space exploration is perhaps less advanced than the sci-fi writers of the 20th century expected. After the Unwinding led to the failure of many of the nascent space-mining companies of the 2030s and the urgency of the SkyComm disaster in the 2040s, it wasn’t until the 2050s that we really began to exploit asteroid resources, with the bulk of them being sent to the moon and later Mars rather than Earth – of course, orbital regulations brought in after SkyComm make it much more economically attractive to leave resources in space.

One of the greatest disappointments of the 21st century is surely our failure to find any other signs of life in the solar system. Repeated missions to promising sites on Mars, Europa and Enceladus, and even long-shot habitats like the deep crust of Venus, have turned up nothing. While the cost of space flight continues to fall, it is increasingly difficult to get astrobiology missions off the ground, with even the sci-fi-inspired trillionaires choosing to place their money elsewhere. Yet paradoxically, we now know of at least a dozen nearby exoplanets where atmospheric signals show promising signs of gas imbalances that seemingly can be produced only by extant life. Now that the Overwhelmingly Large Telescope on the moon is straining at the limits of what it can detect, serious thought is being given to resurrecting the failed interstellar probe efforts of the 2060s, exploiting advances in fusion to build much more capable spacecraft for visiting the stars. Many synth astronauts are already volunteering for such a mission, although it is by no means certain they would survive.

It has been revealed that needless to say, from space exploration to artificial intelligence, our present is nothing like the future that our ancestors predicted, but that has been true for as long as humanity scanned its horizons. The fact that we are living longer and healthier than those who came before us, and in relative harmony with the other people who share our planet, should be applauded. The climate disaster of the 21st century and our failure to avoid it must never be forgotten, but at least we have succeeded in stabilising the biogeosphere. Perhaps, in the next 70 years, we can begin to fully heal it.

Writing about what the world will be like in 70 years could have been simply an exercise in fiction. But by grounding the story in hard evidence, I got real insights.

Just 400 US Data Centers Use More Electricity Than Michigan

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, fresh Harvard research has found.
  • The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom.
  • Sources indicate that federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, fresh Harvard research has found.

The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom.

Sources indicate that federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers’ power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public.

The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers—the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI.

“Hyperscalers have been growing fast, even before the AI boom,” notes Jon Koomey, an energy researcher who was not a part of the study.

It has been revealed that to assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities’ energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities’ carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—the first of which is home to Data Center Alley—were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study.

Industry observers note that “Knowing for certain data centers how much they use over a year is a really useful thing,” says Koomey, who notes that a peer-reviewed study is more rigorous than some back-of-the envelope calculations. Koomey has been involved in a regular report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory since 2007 that approximates the energy and water use of the industry. “Sometimes we know it, but sometimes it’s behind an NDA, and no one ever sees it.”.

It has been revealed that while based on recent data, the study may already be outdated—a reflection of how fast the data center industry is moving. The average size of a facility in the fresh study is 40 megawatts, which is relatively small compared to some of the data centers under development today. Developers are building campuses that are hundreds or even thousands of megawatts, and there are proposals for still larger data centers.

“Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset,” indicates Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study.

The study also does not look at developers who choose to build power plants onsite, known as behind-the-meter power—a factor Koomey calls a “wild card” in accurately assessing total data center power use. Looks for behind-the-meter power generation have skyrocketed at proposed data center sites across the US over the past year, with as many as 189 gigawatts in the pipeline earmarked for data centers alone. Many of these plants rely increasingly on inefficient natural gas turbines. BloombergNEF estimated last week that if all of the behind-the-meter power plants in the development queue in the US get built, it could increase overall US emissions by 10 percent.

Recent findings suggest that while the federal government hasn’t tracked data center energy use to date, that could change soon, and it could be a boon to researchers and the public. The Energy Information Agency, the arm of the federal government that tracks energy use across various sectors, conducted three pilot surveys of data center power use across 10 states this year. Those pilot surveys are now complete, EIA spokesperson Lee Tucker tells WIRED, and the agency is currently using them to design a potential voluntary survey for the sector.

Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let people scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers.
  • Sources indicate that google notes it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web.
  • According to recent reports, dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let customers run scans free of cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let people scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the manufacturer discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with upcoming scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Sources indicate that google notes it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a fresh service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

According to recent reports, dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let customers run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google debuted the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One customers, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

In a recent development, it’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

But perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that consumers want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the firm hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Recent findings suggest that many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

Recent findings suggest that if your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Industry observers note that google rolled out Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

In a recent development, when it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is currently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Aims can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Recent findings suggest that pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Recent findings suggest that ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

According to recent reports, if you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

In a recent development, these updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

Sources indicate that I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind.

According to recent reports, these thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the firm is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy.

WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#459. Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (747 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Newscientist

Massive data centres collectively use as much electricity as an entire US state

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to latest figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids.
  • The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, indicates Francesca Dominici at Harvard University.
  • But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to latest figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, indicates Francesca Dominici at Harvard University.

But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information.

SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike.

Industry observers note that together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that the team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and Newly introduced Jersey. The upper bound of the team’s estimate – 99 TWh per year – would see hyperscale data centres rival the annual power consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan and Washington.

According to recent reports, this vast power consumption has a significant climate impact. The researchers estimate that roughly 54 per cent of attributed generation was supplied by fossil fuel sources, with annual carbon dioxide emissions reaching 25.7 million tonnes – equivalent to the emissions from 67 natural gas power plants.

According to recent reports, the findings are in line with international estimates of data centre power use from the International Energy Agency and are therefore “not particularly shocking”, says Alex de Vries-Gao, a data scientist at the Free University of Amsterdam. “This just confirms the magnitude of the impacts that these facilities are having across the board.”.

But he points out that the study relies on commercial data that is difficult to independently verify, and a set of assumptions on the power use and operating capacity of each facility. “You can’t really validate the results,” he warns.

Yury Dvorkin at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland adds that the analysis is relatively “coarse”, not accounting for factors such as how network constraints impact grid power emissions. “They ignore a lot of nuance,” he says.

“There are definitely a lot of assumptions baked in [to the study],” says Dominici. She wants to see data centre developers and operators be more transparent about the environmental impacts and energy use of their facilities. “My frustration is that as we are moving forward, this narrative is not informed by rigorous scientific data, and data-driven decision making,” she says.

Public resistance to data centres has increased sharply in the US over the past year, with a recent poll suggesting 76 per cent of Americans would oppose the construction of a upcoming data centre in their community.

At the same time, the industry is developing rapidly, with many upcoming facilities now reliant on private gas power generation rather than grid electricity, which increases their climate impact.

Hundreds of millions of people live close enough to data centres used to power AI to feel warmer average temperatures in their local area.

Recent findings suggest that hyperscale data centres reduce the cost of computing power to companies by harnessing economies of scale to run their servers as efficiently as possible. But the larger the data centre, the greater the impact on local communities.

In a recent development, alongside high levels of power demand, hyperscale data centres also require large volumes of water to cool their servers, and take up a lot of land. In Utah, a initiative to build a data centre that would cover land twice the size of Manhattan and almost double the state’s annual peak electricity demand has triggered fierce backlash from residents.

“People might notice increasing land prices, electricity prices, water prices,” says de Vries-Gao. “They might notice an increase in air pollution, waste pollution. This is why people are ultimately protesting. The hyperscale data centres are probably the most painful type of facility simply because of the sheer size of them.”.

Nature Sustainability DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7.

Industry observers note that this earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her latest direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

Recent findings suggest that when all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very swiftly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

Sources indicate that she'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time Upcoming York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that the big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

  • The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that introduced in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept.
  • In a recent development, "I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that introduced in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

In a recent development, "I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, mentioned in a statement.

Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.

According to recent reports, euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music.

#455. Latest Update: You Can Try WhatsApp's Fresh Disappearing Text Messages Early

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (446 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker

Latest Update: You Can Try WhatsApp's Fresh Disappearing Text Messages Early

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (446 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices.
  • As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too.
  • Sources indicate that as WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an crucial account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

Sources indicate that as WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it. WhatsApp also explains that recipients cannot share, forward, save, or take screenshots of View Once text messages. Recipients won't see the text appear in the usual chat interface, either; instead, your recipient will need to open the message in a separate window. Once they close this page, the message disappears.

According to recent reports, as mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That mentioned, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.).

Industry observers note that if you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest revision. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#454. Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1538 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space

Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.
  • Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction.
  • Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.

Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you.".

Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.

According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the "Black Knight Satellite," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.

So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?

Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signals while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.

Recent findings suggest that at the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.

In a recent development, another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.

In a recent development, at the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.

However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the Newly introduced York Times.

It has been revealed that just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well, with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.

According to recent reports, another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies" resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here).

Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.

According to recent reports, arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?

Sources indicate that understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes, proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.

According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.

Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.

That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.

According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview.

At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross stated no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!".

When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand.".

"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.

But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?

"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," indicates Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.

"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email, while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.

Industry observers note that "People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!".

Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.

Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.
